name: Merkle-DAG and content addressing. Aliases and instances: Merkle tree (Ralph Merkle, 1979), Merkle-DAG, hash-linked / content-addressed storage, CAS. Two reference systems: git (blob / tree / commit object model, packfiles with delta chains, SHA-1 moving to SHA-256) and IPFS (CID, multihash / multicodec / multibase, IPLD, UnixFS, Bitswap, DHT provider records, HAMT directory sharding). Neighbours in the same family: Venti, Camlistore/Perkeep, ZFS block pointers, Nix store paths, Docker/OCI image layers, Bazel/Buck action caches, Merkle-Patricia trie (Ethereum).
kind: An architectural pattern, plus two production systems that instantiate it. Git is a de facto standard with a documented object format and an in-progress hash-function transition; IPFS/IPLD is a specification family (CID, multiformats, UnixFS) with a reference implementation (Kubo). Not a browser feature. Not a benchmark - and the absence of any benchmark is a finding in itself.
maturity: Production and pervasive, and simultaneously mid-transition on its most load-bearing assumption. Git is the most widely deployed content-addressed store in existence; its SHA-1 foundation was broken in practice by SHAttered in 2017, git shipped hardened SHA-1 in 2.13, introduced SHA-256 object format in 2.29 (2020), made SHA-256 the default hash for the upcoming major release in 2.51, and is targeting Git 3.0 for late 2026 - but GitHub still does not support SHA-256 repositories, so the transition is blocked on the forge ecosystem and SHA-1 remains the deployed reality. IPFS/IPLD is production for its user base with a stable CID format. The pattern itself (hash-linked immutable objects, structural sharing) is settled textbook material with no open design questions.
license: Git is GPLv2; libgit2 is GPLv2-with-linking-exception; JGit is EDL. Kubo (go-ipfs) and the IPLD/multiformats specifications are MIT/Apache-2.0 dual. The PATTERN is unencumbered and not implementable-around - hashing children into a parent is not property. Nothing here restricts this project, which would implement the pattern rather than link either system. If git were ever linked as a library rather than reimplemented, GPLv2 would matter; libgit2's linking exception or a from-scratch object-graph implementation both avoid it.
keeps_and_discards: Content addressing keeps content exactly - it is a naming scheme, not a transformation, and the objects are byte-preserving. What it discards is MUTABLE IDENTITY, and that is the whole trade. A node's name becomes a function of its content, so 'the same node, changed' is not expressible: it is two names with no relation recorded unless something else records it. Git makes this explicit and then buys the relation back at a second layer - commits carry parent pointers, and rename detection reconstructs continuity that the naming scheme threw away. IPFS does not buy it back at all; a CID has no predecessor. For this project the consequence is precise: content addressing gives node identity that survives MOVEMENT (a subtree relocated in the DOM keeps its hash) and destroys node identity that must survive EDITING (a paragraph with one word changed is a stranger). That is the exact complement of what an xpath key gives, which is why the two compose rather than compete. A second thing discarded, in IPFS specifically: the identity of the SERIALISATION is discarded into the identity of the CHUNKING - the same bytes added with a different chunker, DAG layout or CID version produce a different CID, so IPFS's content addressing is parameter-addressed as much as content-addressed.
structure_preserved: Everything, and this is the pattern's strongest property relative to every other item in this research set. A Merkle-DAG preserves nesting exactly (a parent's hash covers its children's hashes), preserves order (children are an ordered list, and git tree entries are canonically sorted so the ordering is part of the identity), preserves tabular relations to whatever depth the encoder chose to model them, and can represent a shadow boundary as an ordinary edge with a marked edge type - shadow depth becomes a property of the path from the root, which is exactly how the trie key already carries it. The DAG rather than tree part matters: identical subtrees converge to one node with multiple parents, so a repeated component instance across a page - the same card markup ten times in a list - stores once and is addressed ten times. That is structural deduplication that a tree keyed on address cannot express. The caveat is that structure is preserved only as ENCODED: git's tree object models directories and modes and nothing else, and IPFS UnixFS models files and directories, so both would need a domain encoding for DOM nodes rather than reuse of their existing object types.
interactive_elements: Not modelled by either system and not the pattern's concern. A Merkle-DAG stores whatever node record it is given, so controls are handled exactly as well as the node encoding handles them - the pattern is neutral and imposes nothing. The one design consequence worth stating is that whatever goes into the hashed node record becomes part of its identity, so the decision about which interactivity facts are hashed is the decision about which changes create a new node. Putting the tag and the interactivity flag in the hashed record is cheap and correct; putting volatile state there is not (see below).
interactive_state_fidelity: Entirely a function of what the encoder hashes, and the pattern forces the choice to be made explicitly - which is a virtue, since the alternative representations in this research set make it implicitly. If disabled / checked / selected / expanded / aria-* are inside the hashed node record, they are preserved with perfect fidelity and every flip mints a new node identity and rehashes the ancestor path. If they are outside, they are invisible and their changes are undetectable. The token cost is near zero because these are short attribute values, but the DELTA cost is not zero: a hot aria-expanded toggle on a menu would mint a new identity for that node and every ancestor on every toggle, which is O(depth) of pure churn for a change that carries no content. The design that follows for 'tag plus interactivity' earning its keep: hash the tag and the STATIC interactivity facts (is-focusable, role-bearing, is-a-control) into node identity, and carry VOLATILE state (expanded, checked, focused) as an unhashed side property keyed by the same address, so that state is queryable at full fidelity without minting identities. That separation is available in a Merkle-DAG and is not available in a flat serialisation.
layout_awareness: None. Neither git nor IPFS nor the pattern reads geometry, and there is no stage at which geometry could enter unless an encoder deliberately hashed it. Clean pass on no_layout_in_the_fold. The pattern in fact makes the constraint enforceable rather than merely stated: if geometry is not in the hashed record, then a geometry change provably cannot alter any node identity, which is a checkable invariant rather than a promise. Storing geometry as an unhashed peripheral keyed by node address is the natural shape of this pattern and matches this project's stated design exactly.
javascript_required: No. Both systems are out-of-browser storage layers operating on bytes already in hand. Nothing here executes page code, touches a DOM API, or can cause telemetry to fire. The pattern is entirely post-capture.
evaluation_method: There is essentially no evaluation literature, and that is the honest headline for this item. Git and IPFS are evaluated by USE at enormous scale rather than by published measurement: git's correctness is established by the fact that hundreds of millions of repositories reconstruct correctly, and by fsck-style integrity verification which is a genuine internal check (recompute every object's hash, verify every link resolves). What does exist as measured work sits on the periphery: infrastructure and privacy studies of IPFS ('Mapping the Interplanetary Filesystem', arXiv:2002.07747; 'The Cloud Strikes Back: Investigating the Decentralization of IPFS', arXiv:2309.16203; 'Monitoring Data Requests in Decentralized Data Storage Systems', arXiv:2104.09202), and cryptanalysis of the hash function (SHAttered). There is no benchmark of Merkle-DAG delta cost, no measured comparison of DAG layouts, and no study of content addressing applied to DOM trees. Any claim in this item about performance on this project's workload is an argument from the algorithm, not a citation.
corpus_size_and_origins: No evaluation corpus exists for the pattern itself. The largest real-world figures available are from the IPFS measurement studies, and they measure the NETWORK rather than the storage semantics: the monitoring study collected daily-sampled Bitswap CIDs and their DHT provider records over 28 days, producing a dataset of 5.6 million CIDs. That is a large sample of one system's traffic, from one measurement vantage, over one month, and it says nothing about fidelity or delta cost - it is evidence about privacy exposure only. Git has no published corpus at all; its evidence is operational. The gap this leaves is total for this project's purposes: there is no measurement anywhere of how a Merkle-DAG behaves over versioned DOM captures, no distribution of node fan-out, no measured subtree-sharing rate across pages, and no measured ancestor-rehash cost. Those are cheap to measure locally and would have to be measured rather than cited.
reported_precision_recall: Not applicable to the storage pattern, which is lossless and exact - a hash either matches or does not, so there is no precision/recall to report. The one place in this item where a precision/recall-shaped number DOES exist is git's rename detection, and it is the most transferable number in the item: git detects renames in two tiers, an exact tier where a blob's hash is unchanged and the rename is found for free with no false positives, and an inexact tier gated by a SIMILARITY INDEX with a default threshold of 50% (-M50%), reported in the diff header as 'similarity index NN%'. The threshold is user-tunable to 100% to restrict detection to exact-hash renames only. Two independent facts sharpen this. First, the tier-two detection is BOUNDED by diff.renameLimit (documented default 400 in the git-diff manual), and when the rename matrix exceeds it, inexact detection is DISABLED rather than degraded. Second, JGit uses a 60% threshold where git uses 50% - a documented divergence between two implementations of the same nominal feature (eclipse-jgit issue #110), which means 'the similarity index' is not one number but an implementation choice. No false-positive or false-negative RATE has ever been published for either threshold. [uncertain] on whether diff.renameLimit's default is 400 or 1000 in the current release; the documentation consulted said 400 and other sources differ.
independent_oracle: Yes, and it is intrinsic rather than bolted on, which makes this the strongest reliability story in this research set. The verification is: recompute each node's hash from its stored content and children, and confirm it equals the name it is stored under. This shares no assumptions with the writer, requires no reference implementation, needs no corpus, and detects every corruption and every encoder bug that changes bytes. Git ships it as `git fsck`; IPFS gets it structurally from CID verification on every block fetch. Two important limits on the oracle. It verifies INTEGRITY, not FIDELITY - it proves the stored bytes are the bytes that were hashed, and says nothing about whether those bytes faithfully represent the page. And in IPFS it verifies the CID, which as noted depends on chunker and DAG layout, so two faithful captures of identical content can both verify and still disagree. For this project the adoptable form is exact: make every stored node self-verifying, and run the recompute as a periodic sweep rather than a debugging aid.
evidence_independence: Good on the security side, absent elsewhere. The SHA-1 break (SHAttered) was third-party cryptanalysis against git's foundation, published by researchers with no stake in git, and git's response - hardened SHA-1 in 2.13, then a full hash-function transition - is the model of a system responding to independent evidence. The IPFS privacy findings are likewise independent academic work critical of the deployed system. On the other side, there is no independent evaluation of the pattern's performance characteristics because there is no evaluation of them at all, by anyone. Git's own documentation is authoritative about behaviour (thresholds, limits, transition status) and is not making performance claims that would need checking. Net: the failure modes described here are independently established; the cost estimates are reasoned, not measured, and are marked as such.
page_archetype_coverage: None, and none is possible from the existing evidence, since neither system has been evaluated on web pages. What the pattern's behaviour will vary with is not page archetype but SUBTREE REPETITION RATE, and that does correlate with archetype in a predictable way: listing, collection, forum and product-grid pages are built from repeated component instances and should converge heavily in a DAG (many identical card subtrees sharing one node), while article and documentation pages are mostly unique prose and would converge little. The sharing benefit is therefore inversely correlated with the archetypes where CDC helps - which is a genuinely useful complementarity, since the two mechanisms pay off on opposite page types. That is a prediction from the algorithm and must be measured on this project's own corpus, where it is cheap: count distinct node hashes versus total nodes, per archetype.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Script-invariant at the hashing layer - a hash consumes bytes and has no tokeniser, word boundary or whitespace assumption, so CJK, RTL and whitespace-free text are identical in behaviour to Latin. The real locale hazard is one level up and is a classic source of silent non-determinism: UNICODE NORMALISATION. Two captures of visually identical text differing only in NFC versus NFD composition hash differently and become distinct nodes, and the same is true for different-but-equivalent escaping, differing whitespace normalisation, or a serialiser that emits attributes in a different order. Content addressing turns every such inconsistency from a cosmetic difference into an identity split, silently. Git has a well-known version of this pain in filename encoding on macOS (HFS+ normalising to a decomposed form) and handles it with an explicit configuration knob rather than by guessing. The lesson to carry: the encoder feeding a Merkle-DAG must pin a normalisation form, an attribute ordering and a whitespace policy as part of the versioned format, or the store will silently fragment along locale lines.
leaks_outward: The local pattern leaks nothing - hashing is offline computation. The leak arises entirely from DISTRIBUTION, and IPFS is the cautionary instance because content addressing makes the leak structural rather than incidental. In IPFS, requesting content means announcing its CID: Bitswap broadcasts a peer's wantlist to every connected neighbour, and a DHT lookup discloses the requested CID to every peer along the query path, so anyone who becomes a target's neighbour can monitor everything that target requests. The measurement study that collected 5.6 million CIDs with provider records over 28 days demonstrates this is exploitable at scale, not in principle. Beyond the network, content addressing has a subtler intrinsic disclosure: a CID or a git blob hash is a CONFIRMATION ORACLE. Publishing a hash lets anyone who already has a candidate document prove you have that exact document, and for short or low-entropy content the hash is directly brute-forceable - a hash of a 20-character string is not a secret. So a store's hash list is not a safe redaction of its content. Mitigations exist in the research (Bloom-filter and private-set-intersection content discovery, triple hashing, forwarding and source obfuscation, Peer2PIR) but none is deployed by default. For this project, where nothing is distributed, all of this reduces to a single rule: hashes are not anonymised content, and a node-hash index must be treated as disclosing content presence.
mechanism_detectability: Zero. No browser API patched, no CDP domain enabled, no extension, no injected script; everything runs after capture and out of process, so a page cannot detect that its serialisation is being hashed into a DAG, and closed shadow roots are untouched. Adopting this pattern adds no detection surface whatsoever, and unlike some storage choices it also adds no timing signature to the capture path since hashing can be deferred entirely off the capture critical path.
countermeasures: Against hash weakness: use a hash with no known collision path and, critically, make the hash algorithm a versioned, migratable field rather than an assumption. Git's multihash-less design is exactly what made its SHA-1 transition a multi-year ecosystem project still incomplete nine years after SHAttered; IPFS's multihash - a self-describing prefix naming the function and length - is the design that makes the same migration a local decision. Adopt multihash-style self-description from day one; it costs two bytes per hash and buys the ability to change hash function without a flag day. Against distribution leakage: do not distribute, and if hashes must be shared, treat them as content. Against normalisation fragmentation: pin normalisation, attribute order and whitespace policy in a versioned encoder contract and verify with a round-trip test. Against fan-in amplification in the DAG: cap or measure the number of parents a shared node may accumulate, so a change to a heavily-shared node has a bounded blast radius.
measured_fidelity_cost: No measured fidelity costs exist for the pattern, because it is lossless and there is no hardening that trades fidelity. The measurable costs are storage and time and they are not published either. The one quantified hardening trade in the item is git's hash transition, and its cost is compatibility rather than fidelity: SHA-256 repositories are designed to round-trip with SHA-1 content and to push/fetch against SHA-1 servers, and the residual cost has been a six-year ecosystem stall in which the major forge does not support the new format. The cost of the hardened-SHA-1 mitigation shipped in git 2.13 is a modest per-hash overhead for collision-attack detection, with no fidelity cost. [uncertain] on any measured throughput or storage overhead figures for Merkle-DAG maintenance; none were found and none appear to exist.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented by either system, and content addressing makes the omission actively dangerous in a specific way: a paywalled stub and the full article are different content, therefore different hashes, therefore two unrelated nodes with no recorded relationship - the store will not merely mix gated and ungated captures, it will present them as unrelated documents with no signal that they are two states of one URL. Conversely, and worse, two DIFFERENT urls that both render the same consent wall will CONVERGE to the same node, so a DAG built over gated captures silently deduplicates the gate itself and can make a large fraction of a corpus collapse into one shared 'accept cookies' subtree. Both behaviours are correct for the pattern and wrong for the corpus, and both are fixed the same way: gate state belongs in the address that owns the node, and the address-to-node edge must record it, so that convergence at the content layer does not destroy distinction at the provenance layer.
determinism: The hashing is perfectly deterministic; the ENCODING in front of it is where determinism is won or lost, and IPFS is the object lesson. Adding the same bytes to IPFS with a different chunker, a different DAG layout (the trickle option) or a different CID version yields a completely different CID - so 'content addressing' in the deployed system is addressing of a (content, chunker, layout, version) tuple, and identical content routinely gets different names. Git is much stronger here because its object format is canonical and fully specified: tree entries are sorted, the header format is fixed, and the same content always yields the same object id for a given hash function. The rule for this project is git's, not IPFS's: the encoder must be canonical and specified, every degree of freedom (attribute order, normalisation, whitespace, number formatting, which fields are hashed) must be pinned, and the format version must be part of the record - otherwise two runs of the same capture produce a different DAG and the store's identity semantics quietly stop meaning anything.
determinism_across_versions: No browser dependency, so the AX-tree and CDP drift classes do not apply. The drift here is format drift and it has two named instances, both instructive. GIT'S HASH TRANSITION: SHA-1 object ids and SHA-256 object ids are different names for the same content, the transition has been in progress since 2.29 (2020) with SHA-256 becoming the default in the 3.0 line targeted for late 2026, and it remains blocked by forge support - a nine-year migration for a single field, which is the honest cost of not designing for hash agility. IPFS'S PARAMETER DRIFT: a chunker or CID-version default change silently renames everything. AND AN IMPLEMENTATION-DIVERGENCE INSTANCE that bears directly on re-anchoring: git and JGit ship different default similarity thresholds for rename detection (50% vs 60%), so the same repository yields different rename findings depending on which implementation reads it. The operational conclusion for this project is threefold: use a self-describing multihash so the hash function can change locally; version the encoder format in every record; and never let a re-anchoring threshold be an implementation default - pin it in the record that used it.
reproducibility: Excellent in principle and the best in this research set, because a Merkle-DAG is self-verifying: a result can be re-obtained and PROVEN identical years later without the browser, the network or the original tooling, since every node carries its own checksum and every link is a checksum. That is a stronger reproducibility property than 'the algorithm is a pure function' - it is 'the artifact proves it is the artifact'. Two caveats that must not be lost. First, reproducibility of the STORE is not reproducibility of the CAPTURE: the DAG proves the bytes have not changed since they were hashed, not that a re-capture of the same URL would produce them. Second, the encoder must be pinned or the proof degrades to a proof about a specific encoder version's output, which is why the format version belongs inside the hashed record rather than beside it. Git's history is the empirical support: repositories from twenty years ago still verify.
failure_modes: Six, and they are unusually well understood because two large systems have hit all of them. (1) HASH WEAKNESS. SHAttered demonstrated practical SHA-1 collisions in 2017 against the function git had built its entire identity model on; the mitigations were hardened SHA-1 and a still-incomplete migration. In a content-addressed store a collision is not a performance problem, it is two different documents becoming the same document. (2) ANCESTOR CHURN. Any leaf change rehashes every ancestor to the root, so a change to one word mints new identities for the whole path - O(depth) new objects per change, and the root changes on literally every change. (3) FAN-IN AMPLIFICATION. In a DAG, a shared node's change affects every parent that referenced it, so the blast radius of an edit is not local to one path but proportional to the shared node's fan-in. (4) OBJECT-COUNT EXPLOSION. Immutability plus ancestor churn means the store grows monotonically with edits, not with content; git manages this with packfiles, delta compression and garbage collection, IPFS with pinning and GC, and both require the maintenance to be real rather than aspirational. (5) ENCODER NON-CANONICALITY - the IPFS same-bytes-different-CID case, and the Unicode-normalisation case. (6) DISTRIBUTION LEAKAGE - the Bitswap and DHT disclosure described above.
failure_visibility: The best in this research set on the integrity axis and mediocre on the others. LOUD AND UNMISSABLE: corruption, truncation, and link breakage, because every read can verify its own hash and every link is a checksum - this is failure that announces itself, which is exactly the posture this project demands. LOUD: git's hash transition incompatibility (a SHA-256 repo and a SHA-1 forge fail visibly, not silently). SILENT AND DANGEROUS, and worth naming precisely: (a) encoder non-canonicality, which produces duplicate nodes for identical content and shows up only as a store that fails to converge - the same shape as the ingest-degradation symptom, since a store that stops sharing grows faster and probes a larger index; (b) git's rename detection giving up entirely when the rename matrix exceeds diff.renameLimit, which is a designed silent degradation - detection is disabled rather than reported as incomplete, and this is precisely the pattern to NOT copy; (c) fan-in amplification, which has no natural signal. The instrumentation that makes the silent set visible is cheap and should be permanent: distinct-nodes-over-total-nodes (convergence rate) per capture, and an explicit 're-anchor attempted but abandoned' counter rather than a silent skip.
scale_limits: Cost stops being linear in three places. (1) DEPTH, for writes: every change costs O(depth) rehashes and O(depth) new objects, so a deep trie makes small edits expensive in objects even when cheap in bytes. For a DOM depth of roughly 15-30 this is a small constant, but it is a constant multiplier on every single change, and it means the object count grows with the number of EDITS times depth rather than with content. (2) OBJECT COUNT, for reads: the hash-to-location index is the same random-probe structure that dominates the deduplication literature's scaling story, with the same property that its cost is a memory-hierarchy step function invisible to a call profiler. This is the direct link to this project's measured ingest degradation - a store whose object count grows with edits times depth will outgrow cache faster than one that grows with content, and the resulting per-write cost increase appears as time smeared across whatever call performs the lookup rather than attributed to any function. (3) FAN-OUT, for wide nodes: a node with very many children makes its own record large and its rehash expensive, and both systems hit this and solved it structurally - IPFS with HAMT directory sharding, git with tree objects that are simply allowed to be large and are then delta-compressed. For a DOM trie, a page with a 5000-item list is a real instance of this and HAMT-style sharding of wide child lists is the known remedy. The diagnostic that separates these hypotheses is a hardware-counter run (cache-misses, dTLB-load-misses, page-faults) plus an objects-written-per-page metric, not another call profile.
delta_cost_model: PER-CHANGE COST: a leaf edit costs one new leaf node plus one rehash and one new node per ancestor on the path to the root - O(depth), with depth roughly 15-30 for real DOM trees, and with every unchanged sibling subtree shared by pointer rather than copied. That is a genuine and provable O(delta * depth) rather than O(page), and it is the pattern's central contribution: structural sharing means the cost of a change is bounded by the change's DEPTH, not the document's SIZE. CHANGES THAT FALL OUTSIDE THE MODEL, named so the guarantee is falsifiable: (1) A CHANGE TO A HIGH-FAN-IN SHARED NODE - in a DAG the edit is one node but the invalidation reaches every parent referencing it, so cost is O(fan-in * depth), not O(depth). This is invisible in a tree-shaped mental model and is the pattern's most easily missed exception. (2) AN INSERTION OR DELETION IN A WIDE CHILD LIST - the parent's record changes size and must be rewritten in full, so cost is O(fan-out) at that node; a 5000-child list makes a one-child insertion expensive, which is why HAMT sharding exists. (3) A SUBTREE MOVE - two paths rehash, not one, and if the move is detectable only by content the relation is not recorded at all without a second mechanism. (4) A CHANGE THE SERIALISER NEVER EMITTED - CSS-driven visual change, canvas and video pixels, closed shadow roots, and declarative shadow DOM already flattened or missed in the initial parse - produces identical bytes, an identical hash, and is NEVER DETECTED. The Merkle root will confidently assert 'nothing changed'. This is the pattern's most dangerous exception precisely because the hash carries an air of completeness it does not have: a Merkle root proves nothing about content that never entered the hash. (5) VOLATILE STATE deliberately excluded from the hashed record - zero cost, never detected, by design; this is a correct choice only if the exclusion is written down. (6) THE ROOT ALWAYS CHANGES - anything keyed on the root hash (a whole-page cache key, a whole-capture identity) is invalidated by every single change, so root-keyed caching has no delta property at all. (7) The hash-to-location index probe, which is not constant in store size.
reanchoring_stability: This is the item with the most directly transferable answer to this project's one-xpath problem, and the answer is git's, not IPFS's. Content addressing gives re-anchoring that survives MOVEMENT perfectly and EDITING not at all: a subtree relocated anywhere in the document keeps its hash and is trivially re-found, while a node with one character changed has a completely unrelated name. That is exactly complementary to an xpath key, which survives editing and not movement. GIT'S TWO-TIER SCHEME IS THE BOUNDED DETERMINISTIC MODEL THIS PROJECT SHOULD COPY, and it is worth stating as a mechanism rather than an analogy: tier one is EXACT - if a blob's hash is unchanged, the rename is detected for free, with zero false positives and no threshold; tier two is INEXACT and is entered only when tier one fails, is gated by an explicit similarity threshold (git default 50%, settable to 100% to disable tier two entirely), is BOUNDED by a hard limit on how many candidate pairs may be considered (diff.renameLimit), and - decisively - RECORDS ITS CONFIDENCE IN THE OUTPUT as 'similarity index NN%' rather than silently asserting a match. Every property this project asked for is present: exact first, fuzzy only as a recorded fallback, a confidence field, and a bound that prevents unbounded search. The two warnings from the same system are equally valuable. First, the threshold is not canonical - JGit uses 60% where git uses 50%, so the number must live in the record, not in the implementation. Second, git's bound fails SILENTLY: past diff.renameLimit, inexact detection is switched off rather than reported as abandoned, so results differ between repositories for reasons no output mentions. Copy the tiering and the confidence field; do not copy the silent abandonment - emit an explicit 'fuzzy re-anchor not attempted, limit exceeded' record instead. No published re-anchor RATE exists for either tier. [uncertain] on all measured re-anchor rates; git publishes thresholds and limits but never accuracy.
adversarial_exposure: Layout-blind, so invisible-to-human content is hashed and preserved exactly like visible content, and concealment cannot be filtered without reading layout - the same structural exposure as every other fold-side mechanism here, and worse than the heuristic extractors that drop hidden subtrees as a side effect. What content addressing ADDS on the safety side is substantial and unique in this research set. A node hash is a perfect, deterministic, zero-false-positive detector for previously-seen content, so a known-malicious injected subtree is recognised instantly on every page where it recurs, with no model, no heuristic and no threshold. Structural sharing makes this nearly free: if the injected subtree converges to one node, then flagging that one node flags every occurrence. This is a genuinely strong cross-page injection primitive. The corresponding weakness is that it only detects the EXACT payload - a one-character mutation defeats it completely, which is precisely the gap resemblance detection fills and precisely why the two are complementary. Attacker influence on the DAG itself is limited to what an attacker can influence in page content, plus one pattern-specific hazard: an attacker who can predict the encoder can craft content designed to converge with existing nodes, so convergence must never be treated as evidence of common provenance.
provenance_carrying: The pattern is the best available substrate for provenance in this research set, but it carries none by default and the distinction matters. A node hash names content and nothing else - no url, no xpath, no capture time, no shadow depth, no gate state - and, worse, DAG convergence actively erases provenance if the edge direction is wrong: two pages sharing a subtree collapse to one node, and whichever provenance is attached to the node rather than to the EDGE is lost for the other. The correct shape, and it is the same conclusion the chunking item reached: provenance lives on the address-to-node edge, many-to-many, so a shared node resolves to every address that claims it, each with its own url, capture time, shadow depth and gate state. Done that way the pattern is strictly better than a flat store, because the trie key url:xpath:markdown:content is exactly an address, the node hash is exactly a content name, and the edge between them is exactly the provenance record - with the bonus that capture time becomes a property of the edge, so the full history of which content occupied an address is a natural query rather than a separate log. Git demonstrates the working version: blobs are content-only and carry no path, trees supply the name, and commits supply the time and actor.
roundtrip_safety: A fixed point by construction when the encoder is canonical, and NOT a fixed point when it is not - which makes round-trip testing the exact test for the pattern's one real correctness risk. Serialise a node, hash it, parse it, re-serialise, re-hash: if the hashes differ, the encoder is non-canonical and the store will silently fail to converge. That test is cheap, requires no oracle, and catches attribute-ordering drift, whitespace policy drift, normalisation drift and number-formatting drift in one assertion. Git's object format is canonical by design and passes; IPFS's UnixFS encoding does not have this property across parameter choices, which is the source of its same-bytes-different-CID behaviour. On escaping policy the pattern imposes nothing and therefore demands a decision: whatever escaping the node encoding uses must be injective, or two distinct node contents can serialise identically and collide without any hash weakness being involved - an escaping collision is a content collision, and it is far more likely than a SHA collision.
token_budget_and_ordering: The pattern supplies no ordering or truncation policy, but it supplies the two things a budget contract most needs and neither CDC nor delta compression provides. First, ADDRESSABLE OMISSION: a subtree elided under a budget can be named by its hash, so what was cut is identified rather than merely absent, and the model can be told 'a subtree with 40 nodes was omitted, its id is X' and can ask for it - which is exactly the descend-to-expand interaction this project is built around, and it means the child-list price the model pays is a real price for a real, nameable thing. Second, CROSS-TURN DEDUPLICATION: if a node's hash was already emitted earlier in the session, re-emitting its content is provably redundant and it can be replaced by its identifier at zero information loss and zero risk, which is a deterministic context-compression mechanism with no embedding, no threshold and no false positives. Against the recency-dominant position-bias finding, that second property is the useful one: it frees budget for the content that must land late. Ordering itself remains a policy decision the pattern does not make.
representation_cost: Storage overhead is one hash per node plus one link per edge - 32 bytes per node at 256 bits, which for a DOM trie with many small text nodes is a large RELATIVE overhead (a 40-byte text node carries a 32-byte name) and a small absolute one. That overhead is the price of every property in this item, and it is repaid whenever a subtree converges: on repetition-heavy pages the sharing saves far more than the hashes cost, on unique-prose pages it does not. Token cost is zero for the store itself; the token-side saving is the deduplication described above, which is bounded by how much repeated content a session actually re-encounters. The honest summary is that this pattern trades a fixed per-node byte cost and a per-edit O(depth) object cost for verifiability, structural sharing, and nameable omission - and that verifiability is the part that cannot be bought any other way.
what_could_be_adopted: Five mechanisms, and this item yields more adoptable material than any other in this set. (1) NODE IDENTITY AS A MERKLE HASH OVER (hashed node record, ordered child hashes), giving structural sharing, a provable O(depth) edit cost, and self-verification. This is the pattern itself and it fits the trie without modification - the trie already has the address, this adds the content name. (2) GIT'S TWO-TIER RE-ANCHORING, adopted precisely: exact content-hash match first with zero false positives; inexact matching only on failure, gated by an explicit threshold stored in the record, hard-bounded in candidate count, and emitting a recorded confidence field - with the one correction that exceeding the bound must be RECORDED as abandonment rather than silently skipped, which is where git gets it wrong. This is the bounded deterministic answer to the one-xpath problem. (3) MULTIHASH SELF-DESCRIPTION - a two-byte prefix naming the hash function and length on every stored hash. Git's nine-year, still-incomplete SHA-1 to SHA-256 migration is the measured cost of omitting it; IPFS's design is the cheap alternative. Adopt it before the first byte is written, because it cannot be retrofitted. (4) THE CANONICAL-ENCODER DISCIPLINE plus a serialise-hash-parse-serialise-rehash round-trip test as a permanent assertion - the single check that prevents the store from silently failing to converge, and the exact thing IPFS's chunker/layout/version sensitivity shows happening when it is absent. (5) HASH-KEYED OMISSION AND CROSS-TURN DEDUPLICATION in the token contract, as described above. Explicitly NOT adopted: IPFS's network layer in any form (its content-discovery model discloses every request to neighbours and to the DHT path, and there is nothing to distribute here anyway); git's silent abandonment past diff.renameLimit; and git's DELTA-BASE SELECTION heuristic, which sorts candidate objects by type, name and size to pick a delta base - a filename-shaped structural heuristic that would violate structure_agnosticism if copied, and which is unnecessary here because the trie address already provides a principled pairing.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the pattern, with one named carve-out. Hashing a node record and its ordered children imposes no page-structure heuristic: it hashes whatever the encoder emits, and the encoder can be tag-plus-interactivity only. The carve-out is git's packfile DELTA-BASE SELECTION, which sorts candidates by type, filename and size - a name-based heuristic that must not be carried across. Severity: none for the pattern, medium for that one git mechanism, and it is easily left behind. no_layout_in_the_fold -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and better than that: the pattern makes the constraint CHECKABLE, since if geometry is not in the hashed record then a geometry change provably cannot alter any node identity. Geometry as an unhashed peripheral keyed by address is the natural shape here. Severity: none. o_delta -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS with four exceptions declared. Structural sharing gives a real O(depth) per-change cost rather than O(page), which is the strongest positive delta property in this research set. The exceptions that must be written down: high-fan-in shared nodes cost O(fan-in * depth); wide child lists cost O(fan-out) on any insertion, mitigable by HAMT-style sharding; the root hash changes on every single change so nothing may be keyed on it and expect a delta property; and content the serialiser never emitted produces an identical hash and is never detected, which the Merkle root's air of completeness actively disguises. Severity: low, given those four are declared; medium if the fan-in exception is left implicit, since it is the one a tree-shaped mental model misses. no_mocks -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS and strengthening. Pure deterministic computation, no subsystem to stub, no fallback to degrade into, and it supplies its own independent oracle - recompute the hash and compare - which is a real verification rather than an assertion. It makes the no-mocks posture more enforceable, not less. Severity: none. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed -- ADOPTABLE AS-IS. Patches nothing, instruments nothing, entirely post-capture and out of process, adds zero detection surface, and cannot reach into a closed root any more than the encoder feeding it can. Severity: none. OVERALL VERDICT: ADOPTABLE AS-IS in the fold - this is the item whose core mechanism belongs in the design rather than beside it. Take Merkle node identity, git's two-tier bounded re-anchoring with a recorded confidence field, multihash self-description, and the canonical-encoder round-trip assertion. Leave behind IPFS's network layer entirely, git's filename-based delta-base heuristic, and git's silent abandonment past the rename limit. The four delta exceptions above must appear in the O(delta) claim as named exceptions, not be assumed away.
governance_signal_handling: None natively - both systems are post-fetch storage and neither knows about robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF or HTTP 402. Two pattern-specific interactions must be handled above. First, DAG CONVERGENCE CROSSES GOVERNANCE BOUNDARIES: content shared between a restricted and an unrestricted url collapses into one node, so a governance-driven deletion cannot simply remove a node - it must remove the address-to-node edge and garbage-collect only when no remaining edge claims it, which is exactly the shape the provenance-on-the-edge design already provides and is unavailable if provenance was attached to the node. Second, IMMUTABILITY FIGHTS DELETION: content-addressed stores are append-only by nature and both git and IPFS are notoriously hard to delete from (git history rewriting; IPFS pinning and GC), so a governance regime that requires removal must be designed into the store's lifecycle from the start rather than added later. Nothing here is an obstacle for a local store; it is an obstacle for an append-only one, and the choice between them should be made deliberately.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 is the persistent storage of page content, and content addressing does not change what is stored - it changes how it is named, and it makes deletion structurally harder. Three specific consequences. (1) DELETION AND IMMUTABILITY: an append-only hash-linked store is designed to make history unforgettable, which is directly in tension with an erasure obligation; satisfying erasure requires reference counting plus real garbage collection plus, if history is retained, the ability to excise an object and accept the resulting broken links - a design decision that must be made before data accumulates, not after a request arrives. (2) HASHES ARE NOT ANONYMISATION: a hash of personal data is a confirmation oracle for anyone holding a candidate, and for short or low-entropy values (a name, an email address, a postcode) it is directly brute-forceable, so a node-hash index over pages containing personal data should be treated as personal data and must not be exported as if it were a redaction. (3) CONVERGENCE ACROSS SUBJECTS: identical content belonging to two data subjects becomes one node, so per-subject deletion and per-subject export both require the edge-level provenance model rather than node-level ownership. [uncertain] on how EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 specifically treat content-addressed and append-only stores, and on whether a content hash is personal data under them; the direction of pseudonymisation guidance suggests a hash of personal data remains personal data, but this was not verified against the text.
